subject: history_social
passage: Hundreds of thousands of people rushed to California after gold was discovered there in 1848. Because nearly everything had to be brought in from far away, prices in the mining camps were often many times higher than in the eastern United States. A few miners did strike it rich, but economic historian Lucía Ferreira argues that the people who profited most reliably were not miners but the merchants who sold them food, tools, and clothing.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ferreira's argument?

choices.A: Many merchants in the mining towns went out of business within a year or two because of their high costs.
choices.B: Many people who came to California during the gold rush arrived by ship after long voyages around South America.
choices.C: Records from mining towns show that most shopkeepers there earned more each year than most miners did.
choices.D: A small number of miners found gold nuggets worth more than a typical worker could earn in several years.

explanation.why: Ferreira compares two groups and says merchants profited more reliably than miners. The best support compares typical earnings of the two groups: if most shopkeepers earned more than most miners, merchants did better as a group.
explanation.A: Incorrect. If many merchants failed quickly, their profits were not reliable, so this would weaken the argument.
explanation.B: Incorrect. How people traveled to California says nothing about who made the most money once they arrived.
explanation.C: Correct. Comparing most shopkeepers with most miners shows that merchants usually earned more, which is Ferreira's point.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A few lucky miners do not show which group profited more reliably, and Ferreira already grants that some miners struck it rich.
